books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, A. Reform Movements in the Antebellum Period

stimulus.text: "Education, then, beyond all other devices of human origin, is the great equalizer of the conditions of men, — the balance-wheel of the social machinery. . . . It does better than to disarm the poor of their hostility towards the rich: it prevents being poor." — Horace Mann, Twelfth Annual Report to the Massachusetts Board of Education, 1848
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Horace Mann, Twelfth Annual Report of the Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education (1848). Wording checked against the report text as reprinted in Life and Works of Horace Mann, vol. III (1868), p. 669, and the ETSU faculty transcription; ellipses mark omissions.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Mann, Twelfth Annual Report (1848)
stem: Mann's report best reflects which of the following reform goals?

options.text: Religious instruction in every public school
options.misconception: Mann's schools taught morals, but his report argues for education as an equalizer, not for sectarian teaching.

options.text: Schools run directly by the federal government
options.misconception: Mann worked for Massachusetts; his schools were state and local, not federal.

options.text: Free public schools open to all children
Ending all private schools in Massachusetts
options.misconception: Mann built public schools; ending private schools was never his goal.

rationales.A: Mann's report is about education lifting the poor, not about teaching one church's doctrine. Catholic families already feared Protestant teaching in the schools.
rationales.B: Mann was a Massachusetts state official. The common-school movement worked through states, not through Washington.
rationales.C: Mann's 'great equalizer' is universal education: free common schools where every child, rich or poor, gets an equal chance.
rationales.D: Mann never proposed closing private schools. His campaign added free public schools alongside them.
rationales.general:
1. Find the promise. Education prevents being poor by giving each person independence and means.
2. Ask who gets it. Mann's equalizer works only if schooling is universal and complete.
3. Name the goal. Free public schools, open to every child.
Background: Mann lengthened the school year and founded the first school for teacher training.
Remember: 'universal' is the key word — an equalizer that leaves children out equalizes nothing.
